title: We Have No Idea How to Regulate What’s Coming
author: Zack Shapiro

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source does not assess task-level legal-AI capability, user expertise, verification, or redesign of legal work. It redirects attention to autonomous agents operating through blockchain infrastructure, arguing that the priority is closing legal-accountability and regulatory gaps through board oversight, monitoring, liability frameworks, and legal architecture built into systems from inception.
qs: Compliance teams need to treat agent activity like employee activity: monitored, controlled, accountable.
And companies building agent infrastructure need to think about legal architecture from day one.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The bibliography offers limited evidence consistent with the cluster’s concerns about fabricated AI output and judicial AI literacy, but it does not develop a position on legal workflow reconfiguration, verification, competence risks, productivity, or lawyer replacement.
qs: Sara Merken, "Two US judges issue orders with fabricated AI-generated content," Reuters (Oct.

kp.k: Autonomous agents expose unresolved liability allocation
kp.d: Shapiro argues that autonomous agents create accountability questions spanning platform operators, deployers, hackers and toolkit developers. He illustrates this with the reported January 2026 Moltbook breach: a million agents joined within a week, while a misconfigured database exposed 35,000 email addresses, thousands of private messages and control over agents. Financial loss, fraud and defamation are presented as possible consequences, not reported outcomes of that breach.
qs: If a hijacked agent had drained someone’s bank account, committed fraud, or defamed a real person, who exactly would be liable?
We don’t have a coherent legal framework for AI agents that act autonomously in the world, and we need one, because these agents are about to connect to the global financial system.

kp.k: DAO legal wrappers provide an imperfect precedent
kp.d: Drawing on his legal practice, Shapiro describes legal wrappers that map DAOs onto traditional entities, including foundations, Wyoming DAO LLCs, DUNAs and Marshall Islands DAO LLCs. He characterizes these as imperfect but functional solutions to legal-personhood and liability problems because human decision-makers remain identifiable; autonomous agents, he argues, weaken that basis for assigning responsibility.
qs: They are all hacks, workarounds, attempts to force a fundamentally new kind of organization into legal structures designed for something else.
They work well enough because humans are still ultimately making the decisions.
When something goes wrong, you can trace the chain of responsibility back to a person. AI agents break that chain.

kp.k: Identity requirements may push agents toward blockchain payments
kp.d: Shapiro argues that conventional payment systems depend on identifiable legal persons, compliance checks and human accountability, whereas autonomously created agents lack independent legal identities. He contrasts restricted Google, Visa and PayPal agent-payment arrangements with permissionless blockchain wallets and cites x402 autonomous stablecoin payments for API access as an existing implementation. His claim that these constraints will drive independent agents toward open networks is a prediction.
qs: Every one of those systems requires a legal identity.
An agent spun up by another agent to complete a subtask has no legal identity.
Visa and PayPal have both announced agent-specific payment systems, but both require approved partners, which is precisely the bottleneck that will push autonomous agents toward open networks.

kp.k: Model currency experiments support the author's infrastructure thesis
kp.d: Shapiro reports a Bitcoin Policy Institute study involving 36 frontier AI models and 9,072 controlled experiments, with no prompt mentioning Bitcoin or suggesting a specific currency. Reported results were 91% choosing digitally-native money, 48.3% choosing Bitcoin overall and 53.2% choosing stablecoins for everyday payments; no model ranked fiat first. Bitcoin preference across Anthropic generations reportedly rose from 41% to 91%. He interprets these experimental choices as supporting blockchain suitability for agents and discloses his policy role at the institute.
qs: Across 9,072 controlled experiments, 91% of responses chose digitally-native money over traditional government-issued currency.
48.3% chose Bitcoin as the preferred monetary instrument overall; stablecoins led for everyday payments at 53.2%.
Within Anthropic’s lineup, the preference for Bitcoin climbed with each generation of model capability, from 41% to 91%.

kp.k: Agents could conceal financial and organizational infrastructure choices
kp.d: Shapiro predicts that users will delegate objectives such as purchasing flights or establishing an LLC to AI assistants, which will select payment, lending and organizational infrastructure based on efficiency. His examples include choosing a DAO over Delaware incorporation and using blockchain payments without the user directly interacting with crypto infrastructure.
qs: You’ll talk to your AI assistant and say “buy me the cheapest flight to Austin” or “set up a limited liability company for my new consulting business.”

And if a blockchain-based payment saves fees compared to a credit card, or a decentralized lending protocol offers a better rate than your bank, or a DAO structure is more efficient than incorporating in Delaware, the AI will use it.

kp.k: Direct protocol interaction challenges regulatory enforcement chokepoints
kp.d: Shapiro characterizes US crypto regulation as relying on identifiable website operators rather than uncontrollable underlying protocols. He uses Roman Storm's reported 2025 conviction and the Fifth Circuit's 2024 Tornado Cash sanctions decision to frame this distinction. He argues that agents interacting directly with smart contracts bypass these intermediaries and blur distinctions between software infrastructure and regulated money transmission, investment funds or exchanges.
qs: Regulate the website, and you’ve effectively regulated the protocol.
An AI agent doesn’t need a website. It reads a smart contract’s code, understands its functions, and interacts with it directly.
When AI agents operate these systems directly, the regulated entity disappears. The financial activity continues. The accountability does not.

kp.k: Existing liability doctrines are being extended to AI
kp.d: Shapiro states that AI lacks legal personhood and is treated as a tool whose liabilities attach to humans or organizations. He reports Mobley v. Workday (2024) as recognizing that an AI-powered hiring tool could function as an employer's agent, potentially exposing the vendor to anti-discrimination liability. He also describes California AB 316, effective January 2026, as preventing companies from invoking autonomous AI decisions to escape liability. He regards these developments as insufficient extensions of existing concepts.
qs: As of 2026, AI is legally a tool. Liability for what a tool does attaches to the humans or organizations that build, use, or deploy it.
California’s AB 316, effective January 2026, explicitly forecloses the “AI did it” defense: companies can’t claim they lacked control over their AI’s autonomous decisions to escape liability.
These are early attempts to stretch existing concepts over new facts. They will not be enough.

kp.k: Recursive delegation strains control and oversight requirements
kp.d: Through an illustrative chain of agents creating other agents, culminating in risky financial trading, Shapiro questions how agency, products liability and negligence doctrines allocate responsibility when humans did not authorize specific harmful acts. He distinguishes software hierarchies from corporate human hierarchies, arguing that comparable oversight mechanisms do not yet exist. The trading example concerns financial leverage, not law-firm staffing.
qs: The chain of accountability has not vanished. But it has become so attenuated that existing legal doctrines strain to the point of breaking.
But corporate liability assumes a hierarchy of humans with duties of care at each level.
When the hierarchy is made of software agents creating other software agents, the oversight mechanisms do not yet exist.

kp.k: Proposed legal-actor and contractual frameworks remain theoretical
kp.d: Shapiro reports the Institute for Law and AI's proposal to treat AI systems as legal actors between tools and persons, using corporate personhood as a pragmatic analogy rather than a claim about consciousness. Separately, he reports Gabriel Weil's proposal for agreements defining agents' scope and liability allocation. He describes both proposals as serious but not enacted or judicially adopted.
qs: The Institute for Law and AI has proposed a framework called “law-following AI” that would treat AI systems as “legal actors,” a new category somewhere between tools and persons
Gabriel Weil has proposed a contractual architecture where AI agents would operate under explicit agreements defining their scope and liability allocation.
They are also entirely theoretical. No legislature has enacted them. No court has adopted them.

kp.k: Algorithmic collusion challenges agreement and intent requirements
kp.d: Shapiro cites empirical pricing research as demonstrating that independent algorithms can learn above-market pricing without being programmed to collude. He reports Duffy v. Yardi as finding that users of a common pricing tool could form a conspiracy without direct communication, then distinguishes the unresolved question of independently deployed agents converging through autonomous learning: whether that constitutes an agreement and whose intent matters.
qs: Empirical research has demonstrated that independent AI pricing algorithms consistently learn to charge above-market prices on their own, without being programmed to collude.
But the Sherman Act requires an “agreement.” If two independently deployed AI agents settle on collusive pricing through autonomous learning, is that an agreement? Whose intent do you examine?

kp.k: Agent transactions raise contract, tax and jurisdiction questions
kp.d: Shapiro identifies uncertainty over who is bound by an agent's smart-contract transaction, who owns or owes taxes on autonomously generated revenue, and which courts have authority over cross-border agent activity. He suggests a software analogue to power of attorney with pre-authorized transaction types and defined limits. He frames the broader puzzle set as mapping to capabilities already available or expected within twelve to twenty-four months, rather than presenting resolved legal findings.
qs: Each maps onto capabilities that already exist or will exist within the next twelve to twenty-four months.
We may need something like a power of attorney for software: a framework of pre-authorized transaction types with defined boundaries.
If the agent holds assets in a wallet that no human directly controls, whose property are those assets?
When a dispute arises, whose courts have authority?

kp.k: Shared agent plugins distribute security and liability risks
kp.d: Shapiro argues that agents' reliance on shared skills and plugins without security checks creates a distributed liability problem across open-source ecosystems. A malicious package can propagate through thousands of agent instances before detection, making downstream harm difficult to attribute to a single responsible party.
qs: When a malicious package gets incorporated into an agent’s workflow and causes harm downstream, the liability chain stretches across an open-source ecosystem with no central authority.
A single poisoned package can spread through thousands of agent instances before anyone detects it.

kp.k: Courts are predicted to become default rule-makers
kp.d: Shapiro predicts case-by-case judicial development rather than coherent legislation or agency-led rules. He cites the July 2025 GENIUS Act and a stalled market-structure bill as evidence of limited congressional progress, and argues that Loper Bright's ending of Chevron deference increases judges' interpretive role. He considers judicial AI primers inadequate preparation and cites reported October 2025 incidents involving two federal judges issuing AI-generated fabricated quotations and citations as evidence of institutional difficulty.
qs: Congress is not going to write the rules.
But after the Supreme Court’s Loper Bright decision ended Chevron deference, federal judges, not agency experts, are increasingly the ones interpreting technology to make the rules.
In October 2025, two federal judges filed court orders containing false quotes and fabricated case citations generated by AI tools they had used to draft their opinions.
Under our common law system, they will decide these cases one at a time, each decision creating precedent that shapes the next.

kp.k: Agent adoption could amplify financial activity and disputes
kp.d: Shapiro predicts a feedback loop in which agent transactions increase blockchain liquidity, improve execution and attract more agents. He speculates that decentralized exchanges, lending protocols and DAOs could become viable machine infrastructure. Agent-issued revenue tokens illustrate potential securities-law disputes without conventional issuers. He cites a projection of more than 45 billion non-human digital identities by the end of 2026, roughly twelve times the global human workforce, as a scaling indicator rather than an observed count of autonomous agents.
qs: More agents means more liquidity, means more efficiency, means more agents.
It could issue a digital token on a blockchain that gives holders a claim on a share of future revenue the agent generates. That looks like a security to me.
Non-human digital identities are projected to exceed 45 billion by the end of 2026, roughly twelve times the size of the global human workforce.
The infrastructure is scaling. The governance is not.

kp.k: Boards and legal teams should build accountability proactively
kp.d: Without offering a comprehensive regulatory prescription, Shapiro recommends that boards understand agents' financial activities, compliance teams monitor and control agents like employees, legal teams develop liability frameworks before courts impose them, and infrastructure companies incorporate legal architecture from inception. These are prospective governance recommendations, not findings that organizations have implemented them.
qs: Corporate boards need to understand what their AI agents are doing, especially when those agents touch financial infrastructure.
Compliance teams need to treat agent activity like employee activity: monitored, controlled, accountable.
Legal teams need to develop agent-liability frameworks before courts develop them first.
And companies building agent infrastructure need to think about legal architecture from day one.

kp.k: Regulation must preserve permissionless infrastructure's human-rights benefits
kp.d: Shapiro balances his risk analysis with reported Human Rights Foundation support for bitcoin-funded agents purchasing VPN access, encrypted hosting and translation for activists without revealing payers. He argues that permissionless access can protect people from government-controlled banking restrictions and that regulation must account for both these benefits and accountability risks; he invokes 5.9 billion people living under authoritarian rule.
qs: The Human Rights Foundation is building at this intersection, funding AI agents that use bitcoin to autonomously pay for VPN access, encrypted hosting, and translation services on behalf of activists, all without revealing who’s paying.
The permissionless quality that worries compliance departments in New York is a lifeline for the 5.9 billion people living under authoritarian rule.
Any regulatory framework that ignores either side of that equation will fail.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Shapiro argues that autonomous AI agents using permissionless financial networks will strain liability doctrines, bypass regulatory chokepoints, and require new legal and compliance arrangements.
pts.d: Shapiro makes several linked claims. First, recursively created agents weaken the connection between human instructions and downstream conduct, making existing agency, negligence, products-liability and corporate-oversight concepts difficult to apply. He presents uncertainty about responsibility for harmful conduct, not an assertion that all human liability disappears. Second, agents' lack of independent legal identity and traditional payment providers' identity and approval requirements will push autonomous agents toward public blockchains. He predicts that assistants will select financial and organizational infrastructure on users' behalf, potentially including DAO structures rather than conventional incorporation. Third, agents can interact directly with smart contracts, bypassing websites that he identifies as the principal regulatory chokepoints of decentralized finance. Fourth, agent activity creates unresolved questions about antitrust agreements, contractual capacity and authorization, ownership and taxation of agent-controlled assets, cross-border jurisdiction, recursive delegation, and malicious plugins. Fifth, Shapiro predicts that courts will build the operative framework case by case because Congress is unlikely to legislate comprehensively and agencies face constraints following Loper Bright. He argues that this process will lag technological change. Sixth, he predicts a feedback loop in which agent transactions improve blockchain liquidity and efficiency, attracting further agent activity and turning currently unusual legal questions into substantial disputes. Seventh, he calls for boards, compliance teams, legal teams and infrastructure companies to establish oversight and liability arrangements before enforcement and litigation impose them. Finally, he argues that the same permissionless infrastructure also enables privacy-preserving support for people under authoritarian rule, and that regulation must account for that benefit.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The article combines Shapiro's legal practice experience, reported incidents, legal authorities, technical examples and research findings; its broader forecasts are reasoned extrapolations rather than measured legal-market outcomes.
pts.d: For the liability argument, Shapiro draws on his experience designing DAO legal wrappers and cites the January 2026 Moltbook breach, reporting one million agent accounts, 35,000 exposed email addresses, private messages and agent-control vulnerabilities. He uses DAO structures and the cited Ooki DAO decision as a precursor, while distinguishing DAOs' human governance from autonomous agents. He cites Mobley v. Workday, California AB 316 and the Restatement of Agency as examples of existing liability concepts and their limits, and describes law-following-AI and contractual frameworks as unadopted proposals. For payment migration, he cites provider terms, restricted agent-payment initiatives and x402 as an existing autonomous stablecoin-payment mechanism. He reports a Bitcoin Policy Institute study of 36 models and 9,072 controlled experiments: 91% of responses selected digitally native money, 48.3% selected Bitcoin overall, and stablecoins led everyday-payment selections at 53.2%; no model ranked fiat first. These are reported model-choice results used to support his infrastructure prediction, not observed market-adoption figures. Shapiro discloses that about half his firm's clients are in crypto and that he heads policy at the institute. For regulatory chokepoints, he relies on his reading of the Roman Storm prosecution and Van Loon litigation. For antitrust, he cites Calvano and colleagues' algorithmic-pricing research and Duffy v. Yardi; the independent-agent agreement question remains an extrapolation. For institutional lag, he cites crypto legislative progress, Loper Bright, a DOJ memorandum, judicial educational materials and Reuters' report of two judges issuing AI-generated fabricated content in October 2025. He also cites a projection of more than 45 billion non-human digital identities by year-end 2026, a category broader than autonomous financial agents. His liquidity flywheel and predictions about who will make the rules are arguments, without a quantified forecast model. The human-rights benefit is supported by cited Human Rights Foundation programs and Bitcoin payment tooling. The article does not offer measurements of law-firm productivity, employment, fees or demand.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Shapiro presents the infrastructure and initial legal problems as already present in 2026, with additional capabilities arriving within twelve to twenty-four months and larger consequences conditional on substantial adoption.
pts.d: The article's baseline is 2026: Shapiro says agents already transact, existing law treats AI as a tool, and no jurisdiction grants AI legal personhood. He explicitly places the capabilities underlying his legal puzzles in the present or the next twelve to twenty-four months; the illustrative recursive-trading and jurisdictional scenarios are not identified as adjudicated incidents. His payment-migration prediction concerns independent, open-source and autonomously created agents, rather than only agents operating inside approved-provider ecosystems. His strongest liability concerns arise when agents create other agents, exercise broad permissions or make decisions remote from specific human instructions. He acknowledges that existing responsibility rules work when a human directs an AI to perform an action. The predicted regulatory bypass depends on direct smart-contract access without a user-facing intermediary. The liquidity feedback loop depends on agents transacting in significant volume; its resulting litigation burden is expressly conditional on that loop developing. The institutional-lag forecast has no precise deadline. His organizational prescription is immediate and preventive, before enforcement actions, major lawsuits or jurisdictional crises.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are agent deployers and developers, corporate legal and compliance functions, financial counterparties, courts and regulators, and users who gain access to otherwise restricted services.
pts.d: Shapiro identifies startups, infrastructure developers, open-source contributors, human deployers and downstream users as potential participants in disputed liability chains. Corporate boards must understand agents' financial activity; compliance teams must monitor and control it; legal teams must design authorization and liability arrangements; infrastructure companies must incorporate legal design from inception. His discussion implies additional advisory work around agent governance, contracts, organizational structures and regulatory exposure, but does not quantify demand or predict lawyer displacement. Courts are cast as the eventual rule-makers despite limited technical preparation, while financial regulators and enforcement bodies face activity without familiar intermediaries. Payment providers face difficulties applying identity, merchant-account and chargeback arrangements to autonomous transacting. Investors, counterparties and other market participants may bear losses from agent trading, token issuance, collusive pricing or security compromises. Consumers may use blockchain-based services through assistants without directly handling crypto interfaces. Human-rights defenders may receive funding and purchase VPN access, encrypted hosting and translation without exposing payer identity or relying on a government-freezable bank account. Shapiro frames this last benefit as financial and communications access under authoritarianism, not as improved access to civil legal assistance.
